My biggest takeaway after visiting MIT spin-out Formlabs, in Somerville, Massachusetts, and spending time with its co-founder and CEO, Maxim Lobovsky, was that the next era of manufacturing will be defined by advanced materials and digital manufacturing at scale. 
 
One of my long-term interests is the reindustrialization of America. I believe that the 4th Industrial Revolution is in full bloom and this visit to Formlabs was a great reminder of that. 
 
Formlabs develops advanced materials, 3D printing technology, integrated hardware, and software to make additive manufacturing more accessible and scalable.  
 
It was a fantastic visit, and I wanted to share a few of my takeaways from Max:  
 
- Materials based businesses take vision, patience, persistence, and pragmatism. 
 
- Advanced materials and advanced manufacturing are inseparable from the future of American competitiveness, and touring the Formlabs Innovation Hub reinforced that conviction. 

Formlabs is helping build the digital manufacturing backbone of a reindustrialized America. Their work in scalable production systems, and digital workflows speak directly to reindustrialization and supply chain resilience.  
 
- Max described Formlabs’ view of the capabilities that increasingly define industrial leadership: advanced materials innovation; distributed and resilient manufacturing; short cycle-time digital design-to-production integration; sustainable production and circular models; and scalable platforms for next-generation industrial growth. 
 
- There is much in common between how Avalanche Thinking and Formlabs view the future: a shared belief in the power of disruptive materials technologies, manufacturing engineering excellence, disciplined innovation, aligned with long-term industrial strategy and irreversible market trends. 

We also agreed based on our experiences, that the most important progress happens at inflection points where bold moves including the development of disruptive technology, patient capital, and technology and manufacturing leadership converge. 
 
The visit reinforces a core point: manufacturing advantage increasingly comes from integration — software, materials science, automation, and data into production systems that scale. 

Grateful for the opportunity to expand my network and to see firsthand of another American success story in the making. 

Formlabs’ track so far reminds me vividly of the trajectory I found when I started out at II-VI Incorporated in 2004.

I recently posted some tips on how to get hired into Hardware Engineering at Formlabs. That post received a lot of interest, so let me share what to expect if you actually get hired (god-forbid!).

You can find the tips here if you’re interested: https://lnkd.in/eSqb7Ggh

I’ll err on the side of transparency — you can decide for yourself whether it sounds like a great place to work.

You will rarely be handed a narrow task and told to optimize it in isolation.

You will be given problems that span mechanics, electronics, firmware, optics, thermals, reliability, cost, and schedule — and be expected to navigate the tradeoffs.

We debate design decisions hard.
We obsess over product details.

Design reviews are not rubber stamps. If your tolerance stack doesn’t close, if your design adds risk, or if your cost model doesn’t make sense — it will get challenged.

Not because we enjoy friction, but because great products are forged from thousands of small decisions.

You will be expected to:
- Make decisions with incomplete data
- Tie technical choices to customer value
- Balance performance, cost, and manufacturability
- Think in systems, not components
- Ship products

At Formlabs, you won’t just build hardware — you will build judgment.

It’s not the easiest place to work.
We move fast.
You’ll learn to be comfortable being uncomfortable.

However, we are aggressively a meritocracy. If you perform well, you will quickly gain responsibility and more ownership

...and the impact is real — hardware engineers here meaningfully shape products that ship to tens of thousands of customers.

We currently have more impactful problems than people to solve them. We’re growing the HW engineering team by ~30% over the next 6 months — and doing it the old-fashioned way: through operating profits.

If this sounds exciting, we’d love to hear from you:

repost.content:
Very few companies really care about the customer experience. Which is why I can post exactly what we do, knowing our competitors won't bother to copy it. 

One of the things that makes Formlabs sales and marketing special is our Mystery Shopping program. Mystery shopping is most common in retail where companies will pay a third party to come into their store, shop around, and then report on the experience. The good, the bad, and the ugly. Then the retail company uses those findings to improve. 

At Formlabs, Anna Gillemot-Kemeny's team runs this program directly. We have 30+ mystery shoppers all over the world who shop Formlabs e-commerce, direct sales, and our channel partners. And they provide a structured report every time showing everything that went well and could be improved. 

And then we get to work closing the gaps. Sometimes it is a website bug, other times a price quoted incorrectly. Or a slow response from a sales team. Or not writing back in Spanish to a Spanish speaker. Or an AI tool hallucinating something about our brand. It is a long list of "papercuts" that hurt the customer experience.

Fixing these "papercuts" becomes a moat. And it means that over time, our customer experience gets better and better. And it is harder to match what we can deliver. 

The raw output from one of our recent shops for Italy is below. Full transparency. 

Side note - I am EXTREMELY proud of our team's 11 minute sales response time. We have poured blood, sweat, and tears into making that a reality.

repost.content:
I recently learned I conducted 188 candidate interviews in 2025 as a hiring manager for Technical Sales roles at Formlabs. That's roughly three full weeks of my year spent in interview mode and I would do it again in a heartbeat. Building a great team takes time, and every conversation brings us closer to finding the right people.

The best candidates often ask for advice or feedback on the interview process, so I wanted to share some insights for anyone interviewing with us in the future:

1. Do your homework
It takes five minutes to look up who you're talking to on LinkedIn, check our company profile and explore Formlabs' website. That small effort shows respect and immediately sets you apart.

2. Curiosity beats experience every time
No 3D printing background? No problem - most people don't have one. What matters is genuine interest. Watch our YouTube videos about additive manufacturing, explore what makes our technology different, and come ready to learn. Your enthusiasm and willingness to dig in mean more than what you already know.

3. Listen like your career depends on it (because it does)
What we're looking for is actually hidden in my questions. If you want to succeed in technical sales, active listening isn't optional - it's everything. Pay attention to what I'm asking and think about why I might be asking it.

4. Bring your questions - lots of them
I always save the second half of our conversation for your questions, and I'm still surprised when I hear "I already know everything about the role." Thoughtful questions tell me you're thinking critically about the opportunity and whether it's the right fit. Don't hold back.

5. Be authentically you
I know ChatGPT is tempting, but I can spot those generic questions from a mile away (I've memorized the top 3 at this point). I'll also notice the reflection of a second screen in your eyes during our video call. Ask questions that genuinely matter to you, use your own words, show me how you think. This is your chance to stand out.

The best technical sales candidates aren't the ones with perfect resumes - they're the ones who show up prepared, listen carefully, ask great questions, and bring their authentic selves to the conversation.

We're hiring for Technical Sales at Formlabs right now. If you have a STEM background and this resonates with you, feel free to reach out - we would love to hear from you!

To my fellow hiring managers: What's something you wish candidates understood before walking into your interviews?

repost.content:
Last year we received 13,000+ resumes for HW engineering. We hired an astoundingly low percentage of those people, despite trying to grow. Why? Because we already have a very talented team, and we only hire engineers who we think will make the team even better. We take a systematic approach to determining this, but that’s a story for another day.

Given the interest, I thought I would share some tips on how to get hired as a hardware engineer at Formlabs!

Resume screen
- Send us a project portfolio. Whether it’s personal or work projects, we want to see what you spend your time on. We value projects that are technically complex and meaningful to the world. 
- We look for an upward trajectory. Even for entry level positions, we look for growth of responsibilities in internships, growing complexity in personal projects, leadership roles on school projects, etc. 
- List accomplishments and results on your resume, not just things you worked on.  
- Don’t apply to 10 roles, that reeks of desperation! Pick 1 to 3 roles that you think are your best fit. 

The interviews
- We are not looking for the “right” answer to our questions. We are trying to understand how you think through problems. So explain your thought process to us along with any answers you give.  
- If we challenge you on an answer, be open minded. Make sure to ask clarifying questions if you need to, and if you think we are wrong, feel free to tell us! We value differing opinions and have a culture of healthy debate. Just make sure you can clearly communicate why we are wrong :) 
- Try to think beyond the technical solutions. In real life product development, there are many solutions beyond the technical ones. 
- Use concise communication that gets straight to the point

Who we hire
- Engineers who are motivated to a fault by shipping meaningful products, and seamlessly tie their technical work to customer value.   
- Systems thinking engineers who have a specific skill, like CAD, PCB design, optical design, etc. Generalists over specialists. 
- We value critical thinking, decision making, grit, work ethic, and a sense of ownership over specific experience. Technical skills can always be learned by someone who is smart.
- We hire people who we think can grow and succeed at Formlabs on the 5 year time horizon. We never hire someone just because they have a technical skill we could use for the next month.    

I hope that is helpful! We currently have more impactful things to work on than people to do the work. We are trying to grow the HW engineering team by 30% over the next 6 months to solve that problem…and, no, we did not just raise a funding round, we are scaling the old fashioned way, using operating profits :) 

If any of this resonates with you, drop us a resume (and project portfolio) at https://lnkd.in/eewjreFg

posts.content:
Formlabs has some very smart people who are really good at quantitative analysis.  They build amazingly complex spreadsheets and models.  One thing that many people could do better is to try to build models top down rather than bottom up.  Don't start from the atomic element: a SKU, or individual order, complete BoM or whatever.  Start from the biggest picture of what you care about: revenue, profit, costs etc.  Then add complexity only as necessary to capture the dynamics of the problem.

(This is similar in physics to how a problem can be looked at bottom up by the forces applied to an object (Newtonian) or top down by the energy landscape that it moves in (Hamiltonian).  Both are correct, but the energy view can often be far easier to calculate and account for relevant factors.)

repost.content:
7280 mold sets for dental aligners from just two machines in 24 hours?

For this project we set up a fully automated workflow around two Formlabs Form 4BL printers, paired with a wash station and curing machine.

The printers themselves are excellent, but continuous scalable production requires more than just printing. We designed custom baskets for part handling and built a gripper that works seamlessly across the entire process - from printer to washer to curing and storing.

With automated transfers and scheduling, the two printers produced 7280 complete dental mold sets in a single day, without manual intervention.

This setup shows how even a compact cell can reach industrial-scale output when the full workflow is automated. I would love to see hundreds of those machines in a line tended by a robot but it seems like with the productivity they have people rarely have more than 5 in a single room. Automating two of them was great fun. Read more about the setup: https://bit.ly/4oEgdts

What machine would you like to see automated next?
